何家兴.note: A secretary to Luo Yinong who, with his wife, informed on Luo to the Settlement police in 1928; killed by the Red Squad.

贺芝华.note: He Jiaxing's wife (also called Hao Zhihua), his fellow informer against Luo Yinong.

郝芝华.note: An alternate name for He Yihua, He Jiaxing's wife.

谭余保.note: First head of the Red Terror Squad; later a guerrilla leader in the Hunan-Jiangxi border area.

颜昌颐.note: A member of the Central Military Commission, executed with Peng Pai at Longhua in 1929.

邢士贞.note: A member of the Jiangsu Provincial Military Commission, executed with Peng Pai at Longhua in 1929.

张际春.note: Deputy chief of the Shanghai General Labor Union pickets, arrested with the Peng Pai group in 1929.

叶挺.note: A leading Communist commander of the Nanchang and Guangzhou uprisings; later commander of the New Fourth Army.

白云深.note: Bai Xin's younger brother, an official in the Nanjing Ministry of Military Administration; Bai Xin's channel to the Kuomintang.

范争波.note: A Kuomintang Shanghai municipal Party figure and secret-service man who sheltered Bai Xin.

范争洛.note: Fan Zhengbo's brother, killed in the Red Squad attack on Bai Xin.

王容川.note: A man who came to see Bai Xin off; wounded in the attack.

韩云秀.note: Fan Zhengbo's bodyguard, shot in the attack on Bai Xin.

林汉臣.note: A gatekeeping patrolman at Fan Zhengbo's residence.

王宝元.note: A gatekeeping patrolman at Fan Zhengbo's residence.

范梦菊.note: Owner of the Sanmin Photo Studio; he brought the weapons late to the failed rescue of the Peng Pai group, and later turned traitor.

柯达文.note: Ke Lin's cover name as a doctor at the Dasheng Hospital.

贺诚.note: A Communist doctor, co-founder of the Dasheng Hospital cover clinic; later a founder of the army medical service and a deputy health minister.

邵达夫.note: A Red Squad member in the Bai Xin operation.

谭忠余.note: A Red Squad member in the Bai Xin operation.

王德明.note: A Red Squad member in the Bai Xin operation.

赵一帆.note: A Red Squad member in the Bai Xin operation.

吴蓝甫.note: A Red Squad member in the Bai Xin operation.

陈永嘉.note: A Red Squad member in the Bai Xin operation.

左光余.note: A Red Squad member in the Bai Xin operation.

王松生.note: A Shanghai hooligan who peddled political intelligence; a link in the Chen Weinian case.

玉香.note: Huang Dihong's young cousin at his aunt's home in Shanghai.

陈昌.note: A veteran Communist underground worker, one of the Three Chens in Chongqing; see the footnote at his first appearance.

贾绍谊.note: An alternate name for Chen Chang.

刘其珍.note: Chen Chang's wife, sent with him to open the Chongqing intelligence front in 1935.

陈克寒.note: A Communist journalist, one of the Three Chens; later a senior figure at the Xinhua News Agency and a deputy minister of culture.

陈仲英.note: Chen Yangshan's cover name in Chongqing.

刘航琛.note: Financier of Liu Xiang's Sichuan regime, from whom the Communists took over the New Sichuan News Agency.

刘湘.note: The dominant Sichuan warlord of the 1930s, based at Chongqing.

康泽.note: A Blue Shirts leader and head of the Kuomintang's Special-Operations Corps; captured by Communist forces in 1948.

袁福禄.note: Secretary to Kang Ze; the connection through which the Three Chens entered the Special-Operations Corps.

王世英.note: A veteran Communist intelligence officer who headed the Central Special Branch in its final phase (1935).

邱吉夫.note: A Shanghai liaison man for Chen Yangshan, arrested in November 1935.

冯雪峰.note: A writer and literary theorist, a Long March veteran sent to Shanghai in 1936 to rebuild Party contacts and liaise with Lu Xun.

陶敬之.note: A progressive journalist on the Chongqing press cultivated by the Three Chens.

温嗣翔.note: Romanization provisional (scan reading of the given name uncertain); a progressive journalist on the Chongqing press.

侯珍昌.note: A progressive journalist on the Chongqing press cultivated by the Three Chens.

黄应乾.note: Secretary of the Chongqing municipal government, a Zhongtong man.

李鸿混.note: Romanization provisional (the character hun is doubtful in the scan); a Chongqing mayor of Liu Xiang's faction.

袁家佩.note: Commander of the Third Gendarmerie Regiment at Chongqing.

李介民.note: Head of the Chongqing field headquarters' press-censorship office; a Communist defector.

孙中山.note: The founder of the Kuomintang and of the Whampoa Military Academy; conventional English form retained.

红色恐怖队.note: The formal name given the Red Squad on its 1928 reorganization under the Central Special Branch.

武德学会.note: A body Liu Xiang formed to bind his Sichuan followers together against Chiang Kai-shek's faction.

别动队.note: Kang Ze's Kuomintang paramilitary and intelligence corps.

新四川通讯社.note: The Chongqing news agency the Three Chens took over as intelligence cover, 1935-37.

南华通讯社.note: A Shanghai-and-Wuhan news agency the Special Branch ran as intelligence cover.

复兴社.note: The Blue Shirts, a militant Nationalist body tied to the military-intelligence Juntong.

中统.note: The Kuomintang's party-intelligence service, run by the CC Clique of the Chen brothers.

重庆行辕.note: The Nationalist military field headquarters at Chongqing.

政训处.note: The political-training (and intelligence) organ of the Military Affairs Commission; its Chongqing branch funded the Three Chens' agency.

中央社.note: The Kuomintang's official wire service, founded in 1924.

民国日报.note: The Kuomintang's newspaper; the Shanghai edition ran from 1916.

上海日报.note: A Shanghai newspaper Bao Junfu carried folded as a recognition signal.

新蜀报.note: A progressive Chongqing newspaper (Shu being the classical name for Sichuan).

达生医院.note: A clinic on Weihaiwei Road run by Communist doctors as cover for the Party's Shanghai apparatus.

上海临时中央局.note: The Party's provisional leading organ in Shanghai in the mid-1930s, after the main leadership moved to the soviet areas.

海陆丰.note: Haifeng and Lufeng counties of eastern Guangdong; site of Peng Pai's 1927 peasant soviet.

霞飞路.note: A main avenue of the Shanghai French Concession, today Huaihai Middle Road.

城隍庙.note: A temple and bazaar district in the old walled city of Shanghai.

先施公司.note: A pioneering Nanjing Road department store, opened in 1917.

绥远.note: A former province in present-day Inner Mongolia; scene of a 1936 anti-Japanese campaign.

万县.note: A Yangtze river city in eastern Sichuan (now Wanzhou), where Chen Chang was moved in 1937.

扬州.note: A city in Jiangsu on the Grand Canal.

闸北.note: A district of Shanghai north of Suzhou Creek.

平凉路.note: A road in the eastern part of the International Settlement.

赫德路.note: A road in the western International Settlement, now Changde Road.

卡德路.note: A road in the International Settlement, now Shimen No. 2 Road.

威海卫路.note: A Shanghai road, now Weihai Road.

小沙渡路.note: A road in western Shanghai, now Xikang Road.

湖北路.note: A road in the central International Settlement.

西安.note: The capital of Shaanxi; Chen Yangshan was transferred there in 1936.

浦东.note: The east bank of the Huangpu River at Shanghai.

苦肉计.note: A classic stratagem: injuring oneself or sacrificing one's own to make a feigned defection credible.

长征.note: The Communist forces' 1934-35 fighting retreat from the southern soviets to a new base in northern Shaanxi.

全国苏维埃代表会议.note: The May 1930 Shanghai gathering of soviet-area delegates that prepared for a national soviet government.

抗日救亡运动.note: The mass movement for resistance to Japan that rose in the mid-1930s.

ch02.anchor: the National Congress of Soviets on Hart Road
ch02.note: The gathering of delegates from the Communist soviet areas, held in secret in the Shanghai International Settlement in May 1930 to prepare a national soviet government; the source notes it was downgraded from a congress to a conference. The First National Congress of the Chinese Soviet Republic proper met the following year, in November 1931, at Ruijin in Jiangxi.

ch02.anchor: Tan Yubao, just back from study in the Soviet Union
ch02.note: Tan Yubao (1899–1980), named here as the first head of the Red Terror Squad. He later led the three-year guerrilla struggle in the Hunan–Jiangxi border region after the main Red Army set out on the Long March, and held provincial posts in Jiangxi after 1949.

ch02.anchor: another "ruse of self-injury,"
ch02.note: One of the classic Thirty-Six Stratagems: a man injures himself, or sacrifices his own side, to make the enemy believe a feigned surrender is genuine. Here Dai Bingshi lets his own sister-in-law be arrested to allay Communist suspicion.

ch02.anchor: slaughtered tens of millions of Communists and revolutionary masses
ch02.note: The figure is the author's rhetorical exaggeration. The Party's total membership in 1927 was under 60,000, and estimates of those killed in the Kuomintang white terror of 1927–28 run to the hundreds of thousands (a figure of about 300,000 is often cited), not tens of millions.

ch02.anchor: written with a different character, though it reads the same
ch02.note: Chen Yangshan writes the surname with the character 贺 where the standard accounts write 何; both are romanized He. The traitor is He Jiaxing, secretary to Luo Yinong.

ch02.anchor: On the night of August 24, 1928, five important CCP leaders
ch02.note: The book dates the arrest to 1928, but it fell on 24 August 1929. Bai Xin, the Central Military Commission's own secretary, gave away a meeting at his home in the Huxi district, and Peng Pai, Yang Yin, Yan Changyi, Xing Shizhen, and Zhang Jichun were seized; Peng Pai, Yang Yin, Yan Changyi, and Xing Shizhen were executed at Longhua on 30 August 1929. The book's own later citation of a newspaper item dated 14 September 1929 confirms the year should be 1929. Standard Party-history accounts corroborate the 1929 dates.

ch02.anchor: the Hai-Lu-Feng revolutionary base in Guangdong
ch02.note: The Hailufeng Soviet, set up by Peng Pai in November 1927 in Haifeng and Lufeng counties of eastern Guangdong: among the first worker-and-peasant soviet governments in China. Nationalist forces crushed it in 1928.

ch02.anchor: reached Fan Zhengbo, a standing committee member of the Kuomintang municipal Party
ch02.note: Fan Zhengbo, a Kuomintang Shanghai municipal Party figure and secret-service man, sheltered the traitor Bai Xin. The Red Squad killed Bai Xin outside Fan's residence, and Fan himself was badly wounded in the attack.

ch02.anchor: Ke Lin and He Cheng had opened the "Dasheng Hospital"
ch02.note: Both were Communist doctors who ran clinics as cover for the Party's Shanghai apparatus. Ke Lin (1900–1991), under the name Ke Dawen, later practiced for years in Macao and became a senior medical administrator in the People's Republic; He Cheng (1901–1992), under the name He Yusheng, was a founder of the army's medical service and later a deputy health minister.

ch02.anchor: the Shanghai Kuomintang organ paper Republican Daily
ch02.note: Minguo Ribao, the Kuomintang's newspaper; its Shanghai edition ran from 1916. The item quoted here, a false story that Bai Xin had been bailed out and sent to Nanjing, was planted to hide that he was the informer and still in the city.

ch02.anchor: at No. 43, Fourth Lane, Hehefang, on Route Joffre
ch02.note: Route Joffre (Xiafei Lu) was a principal avenue of the Shanghai French Concession, today Huaihai Middle Road; Hehefang was a lane off it. Here the Red Squad shot Bai Xin dead on the night of 11 November 1929, an operation corroborated in standard accounts of the Central Special Branch.

ch02.anchor: the post office beside the Sincere Company
ch02.note: The Sincere Company (Xianshi), opened on Nanjing Road in 1917, was one of the first great modern department stores of Shanghai.

ch02.anchor: toward the City God Temple
ch02.note: The City God Temple (Chenghuang Miao) in the old walled city of Shanghai, whose surrounding lanes formed a crowded bazaar district.

ch02.anchor: Wang Shiying, then head of the Central Special Branch
ch02.note: Wang Shiying (1905–1968), a veteran Communist intelligence officer who directed the Central Special Branch in its final phase; later a general and provincial official in the People's Republic.

ch02.anchor: secretary to the Kuomintang agent chief Kang Ze
ch02.note: Kang Ze (1904–1967), a leader of the Blue Shirts and head of the Kuomintang's Special-Operations Corps (biedongdui); a prominent Nationalist intelligence and political-training figure, captured by Communist forces in 1948.

ch02.anchor: Liu Xiang, the warlord of eastern Sichuan
ch02.note: Liu Xiang (1888–1938), the dominant Sichuan militarist of the 1930s, based at Chongqing; he maneuvered to preserve his provincial power against Chiang Kai-shek's encroaching central forces.

ch02.anchor: run by the Sichuan power-holder Liu Hangchen
ch02.note: Liu Hangchen (1896–1975), the leading financier of Liu Xiang's regime, head of the Sichuan provincial finance department and the Sichuan Provincial Bank.

ch02.anchor: sent Chen Chang and his wife Liu Qizhen to Chongqing
ch02.note: The book's own footnote to this name reads: Chen Chang, also called Jia Shaoyi, a native of Yilong county, Sichuan; he joined the Chinese Communist Party in December 1927 and did underground work in Wuhan, southern Henan, and Fujian. During the war against Japan he worked to turn Kuomintang troops at Changsha, Guilin, Shangrao, and southern Anhui, and during the civil war did peasant work at Chongqing, where the Kuomintang arrested him late in 1948. After 1949 he served in the Chongqing public security bureau; persecuted in the 'Left' errors, he was tormented to death in 1960.

ch02.anchor: the organization decided to send Chen Kehan back to Chongqing with him
ch02.note: Chen Kehan (1917–1980), a Communist journalist; later a senior figure at the Xinhua News Agency and a deputy minister of culture in the People's Republic.

ch02.anchor: the Center had sent Feng Xuefeng to Shanghai
ch02.note: Feng Xuefeng (1903–1976), a writer and literary theorist and a veteran of the Long March, sent to Shanghai in 1936 to rebuild the Party's contacts there and to liaise with the left-wing literary world and with Lu Xun.

ch02.anchor: the Juntong Renaissance Society and the Zhongtong CC Clique
ch02.note: Two rival Nationalist secret services. The Renaissance Society (the Blue Shirts) was tied to the military-intelligence apparatus that became Juntong; the CC Clique of the brothers Chen Guofu and Chen Lifu ran the party-intelligence apparatus that became Zhongtong. Their rivalry was bitter, and the Communists exploited it.

ch02.anchor: the Red Army had ended the Long March and reached northern Shaanxi
ch02.note: The Long March (1934–35), the Communist forces' fighting retreat of some ten thousand li from the southern soviet areas to a new base in northern Shaanxi, after Nationalist encirclement campaigns broke the Jiangxi Soviet.

ch02.anchor: the anti-Japanese struggle of the people of Suiyuan
ch02.note: Suiyuan, a former province in what is now Inner Mongolia. The Suiyuan campaign of late 1936, in which Chinese forces repelled Japanese-backed Mongol troops, became a rallying cause for the national-salvation movement.

ch02.anchor: the news broadcasts of the Kuomintang's Central News Agency
ch02.note: The Central News Agency (Zhongyang She), the Kuomintang's official wire service, founded in 1924; the Three Chens passed its dispatches off as their own agency's exclusives.

ch02.before: In late April 1928, Chen Geng led the Red Squad in person
ch02.alt: A studio head-and-shoulders portrait of a young man with swept-back hair in a dark jacket, looking toward the camera.
ch02.caption: Luo Yinong, born 1902, a native of Xiangtan, Hunan. He joined the Chinese Communist Party in 1921, and in November 1927 was elected a standing member of the provisional Central Political Bureau and director of the Central Organization Bureau.

ch02.before: On the night of August 24, 1928, five important CCP leaders
ch02.alt: A studio head-and-shoulders portrait of a young man in a light buttoned jacket.
ch02.caption: Peng Pai, born 1896, a native of Haifeng, Guangdong. He joined the Chinese Communist Party in 1924, and in 1928 was elected an alternate member of the Central Political Bureau.

ch02.before: After some reconnaissance, Chen Geng and Chen Yangshan learned from Bao Junfu
ch02.alt: A worn multi-story building with many windows seen from the street, with sandbags heaped along its base.
ch02.caption: The puppet Shanghai Municipal Police headquarters.

ch02.before: After Chen Yangshan and Chen Kehan returned to Chongqing
ch02.alt: Two men in padded winter uniforms and cloth caps standing side by side outdoors.
ch02.caption: Chen Yangshan and Chen Kehan.

ch02.before: The agency was up and running, with Chen Chang as director
ch02.alt: A head-and-shoulders portrait of a bespectacled man in a buttoned jacket.
ch02.caption: Chen Kehan in the 1950s.
